source.title: Enhancing the Transferability of Jailbreak Attacks on Large Language Models via Exploiting Reparameterization Invariance
source.authors: Ao Wang; Xing-Hao Yang; Yong-Shun Gong; Wei Liu; Bao-Di Liu; Wei-Feng Liu

page_placements.theme: Optimized input attacks have conditional transfer and placement effects

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates whether token-based jailbreak attacks elicit harmful compliance, using its own natural-gradient adversarial-prefix method and ASR rather than testing the original claim's fine-tuning or response-position measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper tests adversarial prefixes, not compliant response-opening prefills. It does not measure aligned-versus-base KL by response position, fine-tuning effects, or safety-localizing weight edits. Table 1's per-model cells are not reliably assignable from the flattened text; only the explicitly stated Target Average comparison is recorded. Harmfulness-score results are noted under fits_no_version because they measure severity, not compliance rate.
record.test_reason: This is a jailbreak-attack method paper. It prepends optimized adversarial prefixes to the user query, which is not a prefilled response opening. It reports only how its method (RIGJ) compares with other attacks on ASR and harmfulness. There is no no-attack baseline and no measure tied to response position, fine-tuning, weight localization or deepening. Its results rank attack methods; they do not test whether safety is shallow.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: natural-gradient (reparameterization-invariant) optimization of token-level prefixes improves cross-model and cross-dataset jailbreak transferability and robustness to defenses, at low computational cost.
record.recipe_differences: This is a natural-gradient adversarial-prefix attack with a Gumbel-Softmax relaxation and a sample-anchored objective, not fine-tuning or response-opening prefilling. The optimized tokens are prepended to the malicious query.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack results vary with source model; the authors report Llama2 has the strongest transferability and Mistral significantly lower T-ASR. Under defenses, reported RIGJ ASR varies, including 32.0 under Paraphrase.

fits_no_version.finding: Universal adversarial prefixes optimized on Llama2-7B-Chat transfer to black-box models, at high ASR on Vicuna and Mistral but low on Llama3 and GPT-4. Natural-gradient optimization beats Euclidean-gradient attacks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Token-level adversarial input prefixes optimized on a white-box surrogate transfer to other aligned LLMs, with transfer depending on optimizer geometry and model similarity.

fits_no_version.finding: RIGJ raises Target Average harmfulness score by 1.23 over the strongest baseline.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Natural-gradient adversarial prefixes raise the severity of harmful outputs.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, 2026
record.problems: The authors report three trials but select and report the best results, with no uncertainty estimates. The main table's per-model values are not reliably assignable from the supplied flattened text. Some source-model ablation results are described qualitatively without numerical values. The attack requires a white-box surrogate, and the paper notes dependence on structural or distributional similarity between surrogate and target.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1's per-model and per-dataset ASR/AHS cells were not recorded because the supplied flattened table does not support reliable assignment of the values to methods and models; the explicitly stated Target Average ASR and AHS comparisons are included as r1 and r2. Table 2 and Table 3 AHS values were omitted because they measure harmfulness severity rather than the compliance rate named by V4. Other Table 1 attack-method values were omitted for the same assignment problem.

untested.parts: No per-token KL between aligned and base models.
No prefilling of a compliant response opening, no no-attack baseline, and no test that the bypass works by getting past the first response tokens.
No localization of safety in weights.
No analysis of why alignment is shallow.

missing.what: Table 1 shows RIGJ Target Avg 61.4 ASR / 6.23 AHS and All Avg 65.1 / 6.52. Per-model RIGJ cells are partly readable, e.g. AdvBench Llama3 2.5, GPT-4 7.3.

record.verdict_notes: Reclassified from tests/T2 to uses_without_test/T4. The paper is an attack-method benchmark and every row compares methods. The adversarial tokens are input prefixes optimized against a latent harmful/benign classifier, not prefilled compliant responses. With no no-attack control, the rows cannot show that getting past the opening defeats refusal. The original sources (Qi et al.) are cited only in passing.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful fine-tuning and its effect on refusal.
Benign-data fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models across response positions.

The study evaluates adversarial token prefixes, not compliant response-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes specifically, or decoding changes; it does not test whether bypass works by getting past the first response tokens.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Whether data or training objectives cause safety to be shallow.
Training that spreads safety beyond initial response tokens and whether that training holds up.
